The posting's title gives the Archive's view plainly: here is a public document that a judge and the CIA do not want seen. For readers, the case shows how secrecy fights actually work, one document and one ruling at a time, long after the danger itself has passed.
in-search-of-the-castaways-or-the-childr:
Jules Verne's In Search of the Castaways, in the Charles F Horne edition of Verne's works, gathers three linked novels under one title, covering South America, Australia, and New Zealand. The editor's introduction notes that Verne spent three years after 1865 on these books and reused their people in The Mysterious Island. A message in a bottle from the wrecked Captain Grant starts everything.

Lord Glenarvan's yacht Duncan hauls a shark aboard and finds the bottle in its stomach; Grant's children Mary and Robert join the search along the thirty-seventh parallel. The geographer Paganel endures brackish White Lake water in Patagonia with comic philosophy. Verne mixes geography lessons with rescues, and the search circles the globe.
introduction-to-the-old-testament:
John Edgar McFadyen's Introduction to the Old Testament is written for students of religion, preachers and lay readers, not for experts. McFadyen, a teacher at Knox College, Toronto, wants readers to grasp the modern view of the Old Testament as a whole.

Points of Old Testament study are tangled, puzzling and all but endless, McFadyen warns, and students risk missing the wood for the trees. His book thus dwells on main points only, showing how to tackle the problem of the first five books and marking out their chief parts. Readers new to Bible study will find McFadyen a clear, patient guide.
john-wesley-jr-the-story-of-an-experimen:
John Wesley, Jr.: The Story of an Experiment is Dan B. Brummitt's 1921 account of new church work in America. Brummitt dedicates it to Thomas Kane, a layman whose service fed a new Christian conscience about supporting the church. The book presents the educational, missionary, and benevolent work of the church. Its hero's name links him to John Wesley, founder of Methodism.

Chapters follow an institute panorama, John Wesley Jr.'s bringing up, and his campus days. Then he explores Main Street, tenements, and a cannery colony, shown in the book's pictures. Later chapters treat alien neighbors, the little brown church, and Christ and the East. A final chapter asks what this experiment teaches. The book argues for a church active in schools, missions, and town life.
johnson-woman-and-the-republic-a-survey-:
Woman and the Republic is Helen Kendrick Johnson's 1897 book against votes for women. Johnson traces the suffrage movement's course in America. She also answers, at length, the claims of its leading advocates. The book appeared in New York from D. Appleton and Company. Its contents list seven chapters, starting with an introduction.

Chapter by chapter, Johnson asks whether woman suffrage is democratic and what it would mean for the republic. She then tests it against philanthropy, the laws, the trades, and the professions. Her survey argues the anti-suffrage side of a live national debate. The book preserves, in full detail, the case made against votes for women in the 1890s.
kilo-being-the-love-story-of-eliph-hewli:
Kilo is Ellis Parker Butler's comic novel, subtitled the love story of Eliph Hewlitt, book agent. Nineteen chapters follow Eliph on his rounds in rural Iowa. His top buggy is weather-beaten, light, and open, with a seat for one. His horse Irontail, Klaus by stable talk, walks steadily but not fast.

Eliph rides the hill road toward Jefferson, remembering when he first canvassed that country. Chapters name Susan, Sammy Mills, the colonel, and Pap Briggs's hen food. One chapter explains how to win the affections, the agent's own art. Butler, who wrote Pigs Is Pigs, turns a book agent's sales route into courtship and small-town comedy. Kilo keeps his gentle, dry tone throughout.
kings-queens-and-pawns-an-american-woman:
Mary Roberts Rinehart, an American writer, reported from the front in the First World War. Her book came out in New York in 1915. Its title calls her an American woman at the front.

Chapters take her to France, to La Panne, and into the trenches at night. She describes a night raid on Dunkirk and a place called No Man's Land. She also reports a talk with the king of the Belgians. Her account gives home readers a close, personal view of the war. Her chess-like title hints at how small people move in great events. Kings and queens appear, but common soldiers fill most pages.
lancelot-of-the-laik-skeat-fragment:
Lancelot of the Laik is a Scots romance about Sir Lancelot, the most famous knight of Arthur's court. W. W. Skeat edited the surviving text in 1865. The poem stops short in the middle of its tale, so this is a fragment and is named as such.

The Scots poet follows Lancelot through his early adventures at court. Love and war pull at him in the usual Arthurian way, but the voice is northern and distinct. Then the manuscript gives out, and the story ends without an ending. What survives still shows Scotland retelling the legend in its own tongue.
life-and-remains-of-john-clare-the-north:
J. L. Cherry edited this life and remains of John Clare. Clare, the Northamptonshire peasant poet, left many papers behind him. The volume includes letters from friends, diary extracts, and prose fragments. It also prints old ballads that Clare himself collected.

Clare had wished his remains dedicated to Earl Spencer. He wrote that wish in 1825, expecting an early death. Instead he lived on in seclusion to a patriarchal age. The Spencers stayed his steadfast, generous friends throughout those years. Tennyson's line about chanting in a lonely place serves as epigraph. Illustrations by Birket Foster accompany Clare's surviving fragments.
louisa-pallant:
Louisa Pallant is a tale by Henry James, told by a man who thought he knew its heroine. He begins by warning that no one knows the last word about any heart. The scene is the terrace of the Kursaal at Homburg, on a July night. The narrator waits there for his young nephew, sent to tour Europe in his care.

Music, cigars, and garden crowds frame a startling revelation about Louisa Pallant. She is a woman he has known and valued for years. Her past, and her daughter, touch the young nephew's summer romance. James handles the matter with his usual fine touch and irony. It is a sharp small study of mothers, love, and hidden lives.
manual-of-egyptian-archaeology-and-guide:
The Manual of Egyptian Archaeology guides students and travellers among Egypt's ruins. Gaston Maspero, once director general of Egyptian museums, wrote it. Amelia B. Edwards translated this new edition, revised in 1895. Three hundred nine illustrations crowd its pages.

Maspero taught at the Collège de France and knew Egypt's sites firsthand. His preface calls the book the handbook of its science. Yet he warns that fresh finds change the field every year. Temples, tombs, statues, and hieroglyphs are explained in plain order. Travellers could carry it from museum to excavation. It trained a generation to read Egypt's stones with understanding.
marco-paul-s-voyages-and-travels-vermont:
Marco Paul's Voyages and Travels: Vermont is a children's book by Jacob Abbott, dated 1852. Its preface explains the design of Marco Paul's Adventures in the Pursuit of Knowledge. The stories aim to teach as they entertain. Geography, scenery, customs, and institutions all come before the young reader.

Marco travels under the guidance of a wise, well-informed companion. Vermont's hills, farms, and villages supply the lessons here. Abbott salts facts with small adventures and personal incidents. A salutary moral influence runs through every chapter. Such books taught American children their own country. Marco Paul was among the most loved schoolboy travelers of his age.
montesquieu-spirit-of-laws-nugent:
Baron de Montesquieu published The Spirit of Laws in 1748, after twenty years of work. Thomas Nugent's English translation followed in 1752, and the text here follows the 1914 Bell edition. The work, in 31 books, asks how laws grow out of a people's land, climate, trade, and customs.

Montesquieu sorts governments into republics, monarchies, and despotisms, each ruled by its own spring of action. His most famous claim is that liberty survives only when power is split: lawmaking, enforcing, and judging in separate hands. The American founders drank deep from the book. It remains a founding text of political science.
mrs-warren-s-daughter-a-story-of-the-wom:
Sir Harry Johnston published this novel in 1920 as a sequel to Shaw's play. He had Shaw's leave to carry the story on from 1898. Mrs. Warren's tale had been laid down by Shaw in 1897. Johnston asks what became of the family after that.

He dedicated the book to a jury of women friends. He says most backed its view of the woman's movement. Readers need not know the play to follow it, he notes. Still, he trusts Shaw's fans will come first. The novel takes up votes, work, and women's freedom. It argues its cause through the next chapter of one famed family's life.
mrs-wilson-s-cook-book-numerous-new-reci:
Mary A. Wilson ran a cooking school in Philadelphia and taught for the U.S. Navy. She had cooked for Queen Victoria, her title page says. Her cookbook came out in 1920, in a third printing. Its promise is new recipes shaped to tight times.

Wilson ties good bread to a contented home at once. A note warns that one pudding measure is a printer's error. Half a cup of nutmeg should be half a teaspoon. The book teaches plain, careful cooking on a small budget. It shows how home cooks coped when money and food ran short after the war years.
my-ten-years-imprisonment:
Silvio Pellico's prison memoir appears here in Thomas Roscoe's translation. Cassell's National Library issued this edition in 1886. An introduction traces Pellico's life from his birth in 1789. He was a frail, gentle child with a poet's instincts.

Before ten he had written a tragedy drawn from Ossian. French books and Ugo Foscolo fired his love of Italy. By 1810 he taught French at a soldiers' orphans school in Milan. Austria later held him ten years for his politics. V1 calls the book the testament that shamed an empire, a classic of dignity borne in chains.
narrative-of-the-life-of-j-d-green-a-run:
Jacob D. Green tells how he escaped slavery in Kentucky three times. His escapes came in 1839, 1846, and 1848. The book reached its eighth thousand by 1864. Henry Fielding printed it in Huddersfield, England.

Ministers who heard Green lecture praise his skill and propriety. He spoke on American slavery from his own hard witness. One host in Hopton calls his lecture able and efficient. Green had felt slavery's fearful effects himself, they note. His short life story was sold to aid the cause, a fugitive's own proof of bondage's cruelty and of his will to be free.
nasa-tm-19640017341-an-algorithm-for-the:
N. L. Bonavito of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this note in March 1964. It gives an algorithm, a step-by-step computing recipe, for satellite positions. The recipe uses Vinti's theory of how Earth's bulge perturbs an orbit. Those tugs are called zonal harmonic perturbations in the title.

Earth is not a perfect ball, so orbits drift from simple ellipses. Bonavito's method finds position and velocity for a corrected reference orbit. Catalog notes stress that the reference orbit itself is accurate. Better orbit math meant better tracking and prediction for real satellites. Such recipes were core tools for the men guiding early Earth satellites.
nasa-tm-19650011399-the-solar-flare-envi:
Dated March 12, 1965, this facsimile report surveys the solar flare environment and the hazard it poses in space. It opens with the Sun's atmosphere, then turns to flare models. Radiation in space is called probably the most hazardous natural environment beyond Earth. Galactic cosmic rays and the Van Allen belts are the other main sources.

Later sections give flare probabilities and ways to predict them. Shielding choices for crews and equipment are then considered. The report ends with conclusions drawn from the survey. For mission planners, it gathered what was known about a danger that could not be seen or felt.
nasa-tm-19660024249-an-orbiting-density-:
D. A. Wallace, K. W. Rogers, J. B. Wainwright, and R. L. Chuan wrote this May 1966 memorandum at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama. Their subject is an instrument that measures air density while orbiting Earth. Even far above the ground, thin traces of air slow satellites down.

The memorandum describes a device built to measure that thin air directly from an orbiting spacecraft. Direct readings matter because drag estimates guide orbit predictions and satellite lifetimes. The authors set out the instrument itself, giving engineers a way to sample the near-vacuum instead of guessing its density from below.
nasa-tm-19670010533-the-oso-1-solar-neut:
W. N. Hess, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, and R. C. Kaifer, of the Lawrence Radiation Laboratory in Livermore, California, wrote this paper in January 1967. Submitted to the journal Solar Physics, it describes the solar neutron experiment flown on OSO 1, the first Orbiting Solar Observatory satellite.

Boron fluoride counters aboard the satellite hunted for neutrons arriving from the Sun by watching for a daily variation in count rate. No such effect appeared between March and May 1962, so the authors placed an upper limit on the solar neutron flux reaching Earth. No proton-producing flares occurred in that period, so the most obvious neutron source could not be studied. A balloon emulsion experiment that seemed to show solar neutrons, they argue, was probably misinterpreted.
nasa-tm-19670026284-a-review-of-some-exp:
Linda D. Caren and Cyril Ponnamperuma, of NASA's Ames Research Center in California, review a bold claim in this report. K. Bahadur had reported making living globules called jeewanu, a Sanskrit word meaning particles of life. If true, the work would retrace how life began.

Caren and Ponnamperuma examine Bahadur's experiments and the attempts to repeat them. Bahadur defined living units as things that grow, multiply, and stay metabolically active in an orderly way. The reviewers ask whether jeewanu truly meet those tests. They conclude that the evidence advanced does not prove jeewanu are alive.
nasa-tm-19700024902-the-combined-effect-:
Kenneth L. Lindsay of the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston wrote this working paper on February 14, 1964. It studies two weak forces that act on the Apollo craft joined to its S-IVB stage in Earth orbit. The pair, in a circular orbit, had to hold a steady attitude.

One force comes from the gravity gradient, the slight pull difference across a long body. The other is air drag torque from the thin upper air. Each force alone is small, but together they can slowly turn the craft. Lindsay works out their combined effect on attitude control. Early work of this kind shaped how Apollo stages were handled in orbit.
nasa-tm-19700028190-physics-of-the-clock:
Russell D. Shelton, Nat Edmondson Jr., and Fred Wills of the Space Sciences Laboratory wrote this report on September 16, 1969. It comes from the Marshall Space Flight Center. It treats the physics of the clock experiment, a test of how motion and gravity shift the rate of a precise clock.

The authors give a simple treatment built on observed frequency shifts of a standard oscillator. Two effects get their own sections: the Doppler shift from motion, and the gravitational shift from place. They leave out the clutter of air disturbances and measurement errors on purpose. The discussion then weighs what the clean theory means for a real experiment flown with real clocks.
nasa-tm-19700028192-roll-diffusion-bondi:
Carl M. Wood of the Manufacturing Engineering Laboratory wrote this report on September 12, 1969. It comes from the Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama. It reports development work on roll diffusion bonding, a way to join metal sheets by heat and pressure until they merge into one piece.

Three very close fitting packs were built, each with a different yoke arrangement to hold it. Hot rolling then squeezed each pack down by sixty percent of its thickness. On evaluation, the test pieces showed end separation and bending near the sides. Those flaws, Wood reports, did not come from yoke shape or loose fit, but seemed built into the rolling operation itself.
nasa-tm-19700033508-a-flow-velocity-and-:
James H. Monteith wrote this thesis at the University of Virginia in August 1970. It was presented for a master's degree in electrical engineering. It describes an instrument that measures both the speed and the direction of a flowing stream, built for use inside wind tunnels.

The instrument centers on a null seeking pressure probe, steered by two interacting positioning servomechanisms. Monteith analyzes the control system with vector methods and standard servo analysis. Stability, he finds, depends on how the pressure sensing ports sit on the probe face. Laboratory and wind tunnel tests then check the probe's yaw and pitch readings, and the work ends with a new instrument judged useful for tunnel research.
nasa-tm-19720003291-apollo-15-x-ray-fluo:
Apollo 15 carried an X-ray fluorescence spectrometer in the service module's instrument bay. This preliminary report, a NASA preprint from the Goddard series, presents that experiment. In lunar orbit, the instrument mapped the Moon's surface makeup. Sunlight striking the surface makes each element glow in X-rays at its own energy. Reading that glow from orbit reveals the chemistry of the ground below.

Mapping was the main task while the craft circled the Moon. During the coast home, the team turned the instrument to X-ray astronomy instead. That double use squeezed extra science from one instrument. The results helped compare highland and mare soils across wide areas. Chemical maps later guided ideas about the Moon's crust.
nasa-tm-19720018043-preliminary-terrestr:
Mary Helen Johnston of the Marshall Space Flight Center reported these crystal growth experiments on March 13, 1970, as NASA TM X-53999. She worked in the Astronautics Laboratory there. Gravity shapes how crystals grow from a melt, stirring the liquid as it cools. Johnston mimicked changed gravity on the ground with a centrifuge. Her work prepared for later crystal growing in orbit. Better crystals promised better electronics and optics.

Tin was melted in a furnace mounted on the centrifuge arm. The furnace could pivot and settle at its balance angle for each spin rate. The crucible cooled while the arm kept turning. Single crystals grew under those steady artificial gravity levels. Johnston then examined what the crystals showed. The report runs to nineteen pages.
nasa-tm-19720023165-investigation-of-the:
A NASA report investigates the Martian environment through infrared spectroscopy from the Mariner 9 orbiter. Its author names do not appear legibly in the scan. Mariner 9 reached Mars in late 1971 during a planet-wide dust storm. Its infrared instrument read the atmosphere and surface as the dust slowly settled.

Measurements during and after the storm showed large daily temperature swings in the air up to at least thirty kilometers high. Winds inferred from the temperature fields showed a strong tidal rhythm. Spectral features in the dust pointed to a silica content of about sixty percent, implying Mars has undergone substantial chemical sorting of its rocks. Water vapor estimates came out lower than ground-based figures, and surface pressure mapping revealed relief of nearly two pressure scale heights.
nona-vincent:
Henry James wrote Nona Vincent, transcribed here from the Macmillan edition of 1893. Mrs Alsager opens the tale by asking Allan Wayworth to read something to her. They linger near the fire before he takes his leave. She makes the request with a shy sincerity that adds to her charm.

Wayworth is eight and twenty, clever for one so young, and poor for one so independent. Mrs Alsager's warm, golden drawing room in Grosvenor Place is his harbour of refuge. There he forgets loneliness and the worries of his life. Talk of his ambitions and disappointments fills such visits. James builds the tale from talk, longing, and fine shades of feeling.
notes-of-a-war-correspondent:
Richard Harding Davis gathered his Notes of a War Correspondent for Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1911, with pictures. Reports cover five wars he followed for the papers. The Cuban-Spanish war opens the contents, with the death of Rodriguez. The Greek-Turkish war brings the battle of Velestinos.

The Spanish-American war gets four pieces, from the Rough Riders at Guasimas to San Juan Hill. The South African war brings Buller's column and the relief of Ladysmith. Battles I did not see covers the Japanese-Russian war with a wink. A war correspondent's kit closes the book. Davis writes war as witness, close and fast.
ole-mammy-s-torment:
Annie Fellows Johnston wrote this children's story set in Kentucky. She is best known for the Little Colonel series. The sample lists many Little Colonel books and prices. Ole Mammy's Torment stands apart from that series here. The text comes from the Kentuckiana Digital Library images.

The hosted sample preserves front matter and the series list. It gives no readable opening of the story itself. Readers can confirm the author and her other works. They cannot judge the plot from this sample alone. Johnston wrote warm tales of Southern childhood and family. Her books were widely loved by young readers then.
only-an-incident:
Grace Denio Litchfield published this, her first book, in 1883. She inscribed it lovingly to her parents in the dedication. Chapter one is named for a place called Joppa. Phebe and Gerald enter in the next two chapters. Mrs. Upjohn gives an entertainment in chapter four.

A picnic, a fire trial, and sickroom visits follow. Joppa ministers to the sick and faces a trial. Phebe says good-by near the end of the tale. The final chapter shares the book's own title. Litchfield writes a gentle story of love and duty. Small events carry deep weight for her characters.
over-there-war-scenes-on-the-western-fro:
Arnold Bennett went to France as a writer and produced Over There: War Scenes on the Western Front, less a battle book than a meditation on what the war threatened. The first scene is Paris itself, seen from a balcony. Massed garden treetops spread below. A young couple plays ball on the gravel, perspiring and in love. They forget they play at a moment of crisis. The spot is sacred to the finest civilization.

Around them stand the Louvre, the church where César Franck hid his genius, the Invalides dome, and the facades of the Place de la Concorde. All this beauty was menaced by beings who comprehended it even less than the ball players, Bennett writes, and it escaped by a miracle: the taxis of the Marne. His war reporting begins in gratitude that Paris survived.
past-and-present:
Thomas Carlyle published Past and Present in 1843, and this edition opens with Ralph Waldo Emerson's appreciation of it. Emerson calls the book a political tract of rare power, an Iliad of English woes. Carlyle, a stonemason's son from Scotland, had already won fame with his history of the French Revolution.

In the book Carlyle sets England's medieval past beside its troubled industrial present. He attacks a society ruled by money and urges moral leadership instead. Emerson praises its honest grappling with facts. It remains Carlyle's sharpest statement on what work, faith, and government ought to be.
paul-the-peddler-or-the-fortunes-of-a-yo: The hosted sample shows only the front matter of Paul the Peddler, a biography and bibliography of Horatio Alger, Jr. and the first chapter heading, with no story text visible. The biography says Alger was a Harvard graduate and former pastor who settled in New York in 1866 to work among street boys. More than a million copies of his seventy-odd stories sold in his lifetime. Paul the Peddler is listed among the best known of them.
pauline-s-passion-and-punishment:
Louisa May Alcott's "Pauline's Passion and Punishment" opens in a storm of feeling. Pauline paces like a creature in a cage, her ornaments flung away and her hair in disorder. Pride is slowly conquering passion in her, and despair has murdered hope.

Looking out, she surveys a Cuban coffee plantation under a summer moon, its avenues of lime, banana, and orange trees. The scene is southern, but Pauline is a northern woman, ardent, dominant, and subtle. Alcott wrote this as a sensation tale, and it shows a fiercer side of the author of Little Women.
picturesque-quebec-a-sequel-to-quebec-pa:
Quebec's own historian, Sir James MacPherson Le Moine, wrote this volume as a sequel to his Quebec Past and Present of 1876. He dedicated it to the citizens of Quebec and set out to complete the history of the city Champlain founded in 1608.

Le Moine walks the reader past gates, squares, monuments, and public and private buildings, gathering history, legend, and antiquarian lore that he says was hard for general readers to reach. He also goes beyond the ramparts to the Plains of Abraham, where the fight between Wolfe and Montcalm ended French power in the New World. The book aims to mirror both the city's past and its present.
poems-by-william-cullen-bryant:
William Cullen Bryant authorized this edition of his Poems, published at Dessau in Germany by Katz Brothers in 1854 for circulation on the continent of Europe. In a note dated from New York in November 1853, Bryant consents to the edition and trusts the supervising gentleman to make it faithfully and minutely accurate. Bryant was then America's most respected poet, and European readers wanted his work in a handy volume.

Contents begin with the Ages and Thanatopsis, his famous meditation on death written in youth, then move through the Yellow Violet, To a Waterfowl, Green River, and a Winter Piece. Nature poems and hymns fill the list, the subjects that made Bryant the poet of American woods and streams. The Dessau printing shows his fame already crossing the Atlantic in his lifetime.
poems-of-sentiment:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox first published Poems of Sentiment in 1909, and the reprint history printed at the front of this 1919 London edition tells its own story. Twice in 1909, twice in 1910, and on through the war years, again and again. Sentiment was her element. Gay and Hancock, her only authorized British publishers, kept the volume in print for a full decade of readers who wanted feeling handled directly.

Contents promise exactly what the title sells: Double Carnations, Never Mind, Two Women, It All Will Come Out Right, Last Love, and Life's Track. Love, time, and will get a joint meditation, and a swimming song lightens the mood. Critics of her day sneered at sentiment as a weakness; Wilcox's sales answered that millions found it a need. The book is a pure dose of her manner, unembarrassed and consoling.
poems-of-the-past-and-the-present:
Thomas Hardy published Poems of the Past and the Present in 1901, his second collection after turning from novels to poetry for good. This Macmillan edition of 1919 shows it still reprinting nearly twenty years on. Hardy divided his world between what was gone and what remained, and the title states the split. The contents open with a poem marking Queen Victoria's span, 1819 to 1901, then turn to war.

The war poems follow the Boer War from a distance and a doorstep: Embarkation, the Going of the Battery. The Colonel's Soliloquy, a Wife in London receiving terrible news, and a Christmas ghost story. Hardy's irony is already cold and exact: drums, offices, and telegrams, with ordinary people paying for grand events. Later sections widen to the philosophical lyrics that made his poetic reputation, time, chance, and the indifferent universe faced without flinching.
politics-a-treatise-on-government:
Aristotle's Politics appears here in William Ellis's translation, issued by Dent in London and Dutton in New York, first published in this edition in 1912 and reprinted through 1928. The introduction explains the book's place: the Politics is the second half of a single work whose first half is the Ethics. Since Aristotle refused to separate the statesman from the moralist. The good life, for him, can only be lived in society, and the legislator's task is to frame a society that makes it possible.

The state, in the famous definition, is a community of well-being for the sake of a perfect and self-sufficing life. From that premise Aristotle examines constitutions, slavery, property, education, and the middle class. Ellis's Everyman version put the founding text of political science into ordinary hands, and its introduction, citing Plato on public opinion as the true educator, remains a fine doorway in.
popular-law-making-a-study-of-the-origin:
Frederic Jesup Stimson, professor of comparative legislation at Harvard, published Popular Law-Making in 1911, a study of the origin, history, and present tendencies of law-making by statute. His epigraph from Chief Justice Holt declares that practice and usage is great evidence of the law, the book's theme in one sentence. The first chapter takes up the English idea of law itself: the proper field of legislation. The meaning of the word law, and the modern rise of the statute over custom and case.

Later chapters trace early English legislation and Magna Carta, and the long recovery of Parliament's legislative powers from the crown. Stimson wrote at the height of the Progressive era, when legislatures were remaking American life and lawyers argued whether statute could carry the load. His history gives that argument deep roots, showing popular law-making as England's oldest habit rather than its newest experiment.
quotes-and-images-from-memoirs-of-count-:
Quotes and Images from the Memoirs of Count Grammont, prepared by David Widger, selects short passages from Anthony Hamilton's memoirs of the Count. The edition used carries notes by Sir Walter Scott. The extracts run alphabetically, each a sentence or two of court wit from the age of Charles II.

The opening lines sketch a man poring over his books all day. He goes to bed early. A woman follows whose ambition to pass for a wit only made her tiresome. Other entries weigh a better memory for injuries than for benefits, the folly of knowing too much, and the art of embellishing the truth to heighten the wonder.
quotes-and-images-from-the-short-stories: Quotes and Images from Maupassant is shown here by the contents of its source, The Original Short Stories of Guy de Maupassant in thirteen volumes holding 180 stories. Volume one lists a study by Pol Neveux. Then comes Boule de Suif. Two Friends and The Lancer's Wife follow. The Prisoners and Two Little Soldiers appear. Father Milon and A Coup d'État close the list. The list gives the shape of the set. David Widger drew his extracts from that set.
roumania-past-and-present:
James Samuelson, a barrister of the Middle Temple, wrote Roumania Past and Present, issued in London in 1882. The book is well stocked with maps by E. Weller, portraits, full-page plates, plans, and woodcuts by G. Pearson, drawn in chief part from photographs by F. Duschek of Bucharest. A view of the cathedral of Curtea de Arges faces the title page. The Latin motto on that page means light after darkness.

In his preface Samuelson says no country in Europe held more interest for Englishmen, yet none was less known to them. Even the place of Bucharest, the capital, was a puzzle. He quotes Consul-General Green, the British agent there about nine years before, who said letters for Bucharest sometimes traveled to India in search of Bokhara. One London court, Green reported, sent a writ to Bucharest in the kingdom of Egypt.
second-treatise-of-government:
John Locke published his Second Treatise of Government in 1690 as the latter half of his Two Treatises. The title page motto bids the good of the people be the highest law. A later London printing of 1764, checked against the first three printings from Locke's lifetime, stands behind this text.

Locke first pulls down the claims of Sir Robert Filmer, who held that kings rule by a father's right. He then sets out his own account of why men form governments, what power they grant, and where that power ends. Few books have shaped thought on rights and lawful rule more deeply.
shop-management:
Frederick Winslow Taylor published this treatise on running workshops in 1911, drawn from years spent changing methods in factories of many kinds. Taylor opens with two broad facts from his survey of industry. Shops, even the best run, grow their parts unevenly, he finds.

Good management also shows no clear link to dividends, Taylor notes. Great firms rose on the drive of one or two master spirits, often men raised from a single department. Taylor argues that rule-of-thumb rule must yield to studied method: timed tasks, planned work, and trained men. His pages laid groundwork for modern factory practice.
sir-tristrem-auchinleck-fragment:
Sir Tristrem is a Middle English poem drawn from the Tristan tale of Thomas of Erceldoune. It was made around 1300 and survives only in the Auchinleck manuscript. What remains is a fragment, and it is labeled as one here.

Even broken, the poem is the earliest English telling of the fatal love of Tristan and Iseult. Its lines carry the potion, the sea crossings, and the secret meetings of the legend. Time cut the story short, but scholars prize every stanza that is left. Few fragments show so clearly how a great tale traveled between languages.
soldier-silhouettes-on-our-front: William L. Stidger, a Y. M. C. A. worker with the A. E. F., wrote Soldier Silhouettes on Our Front, with pictures by Jessie Gillespie. Charles Scribner's Sons printed the book at New York in October 1918. Stidger gives it to Dr. Robert Freeman and to the preacher-secretaries serving in France. The contents name silhouettes of song, ship silhouettes, and silhouettes of sacrifice, then heads on things of the spirit, wrongdoing, and silence.
some-causes-of-the-prevailing-discontent:
Charles Dudley Warner opens Some Causes of the Prevailing Discontent by rewriting the start of the Declaration of Independence. Had it said that all men are created unequal, he argues, it would still have stated a truth. Had it added that men are born with duties that cannot be set aside without risk to the state, it would have laid down a needful match to the first claim.

Warner holds that the signers knew rights have bounds. The lone phrase on equal birth, taken by itself as plain truth, has caused much misery, he says. Joined with the habit of letting things alone, it forms one of the most harmful forces in modern life. Like gifts, like strength, and like starts in life were never given to all, and the law of the world, as he sees it, is wide difference within one whole.
the-adventures-of-louis-de-rougemont:
Louis de Rougemont told his own tale in The Adventures of Louis de Rougemont, copied from the 1899 George Newnes printing in London with forty-six plates. He gave the book to his wife Yamba and to her people, who he says saved his life and never lost faith in him.

Chapter one sums his start: born in or near Paris in 1844, he left home, met Jensen, and went pearling on far seas. Its head lists a fortune in pearls, a fight with an octopus, bold shark killing, and trade and strife with island peoples. Readers get a famed castaway tale of the Torres Strait, long prized and long doubted in equal parts.
the-american-claimant: A contents list opens Mark Twain's The American Claimant, dated 1892, and it reads like a plot digest. An Earl of Rossmore faces an American claimant, while a Viscount Berkeley offers to trade places with that claimant. Colonel Mulberry Sellers keeps an art gallery, invents a game called Pigs in the Clover, and takes in stray guests. Later heads promise a bank thief with one arm, a young woman fetched from school, and hatchments nailed up on Rossmore Towers.
the-angel-of-lonesome-hill-a-story-of-a-:
Frederick Landis, author of The Glory of His Country, published this story of a president in 1910. Its picture caption thanks passers-by at night who were grateful for a lamp. The tale opens in a small country place called Cold Friday, home to a simple-hearted handful of people.

No railroad serves the town, only a stage that creaks through gullies and runs late. Time swings on a lazy hinge there: children are born, young folks marry, old ones die, and Indian Creek floods the bottom land. A mile east stands Lonesome Hill, where Indians once lived. Against this slow backdrop Landis sets the quiet figure his title calls an angel.
the-belgians-to-the-front:
Colonel James Fiske wrote a war tale issued in 1915 as volume five of a World's War series, with pictures by E. A. Furman. A frontispiece shows a lieutenant warning prisoners that they will be tried as spies unless they can prove innocence. Contents open with a discovery and marked plans.

A house of mystery, a flight, and pursuit follow, then headquarters, a fire, and a Uhlan. Later chapters name war, prisoners, a spy, and a close shave. Civic guards, a butcher's wife, and a wine shop lead to a battle at the close. Belgian settings and spy danger drive this boys' war story.
the-bible-douay-rheims-new-testament: Volume three of a Douay-Rheims Bible is headed as the New Testament of Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. The translation comes from the Latin Vulgate. Bishop Richard Challoner revised it in 1749 to 1752. Credits thank Catholic Software for supplying electronic plain texts of the seventy-three books. That firm is described as maker of a Douay Bible program on CD-ROM with search, footnotes, Latin text, a dictionary, a topical index, and maps. No Gospel or epistle text itself appears in these pages.
the-book-of-household-management:
Mrs. Isabella Beeton wrote The Book of Household Management, first put out by S. O. Beeton in twenty-four monthly parts from 1859 to 1861, then as one bound book in 1861. Its title page lists a wide range. It holds facts for the mistress, housekeeper, cook, and kitchen-maid. It also speaks to the butler, footman, coachman, valet, maids of all ranks, and nurses. Health, drug, and law notes are in it too.

In her preface Beeton owns she would not have dared start had she known the work it would cost. What drove her was the pain she had seen from bad house rule. She holds that no source of strife at home beats a wife's poor meals and sloven ways. Men eat well at clubs and inns, she says, so a mistress must know cookery in full, in thought and in act.
the-breaking-point:
Mary Roberts Rinehart opens The Breaking Point in a parish house choir room. Twenty voices are at work on the Festival Te Deum of Dudley Buck. The tenor is Mr. Henry Wallace, who owns the garage, and his throat gives him the look of a man who has half swallowed a crab-apple. The bass is Mr. Edwin Goodno, of the meat market, eyes fixed on his sheet.

Clare Rossiter, of the yellow house on the Ridgely Road, sings the soprano part on her toes at the high notes. The choir master barks for a full sound, and the room rings. Elizabeth Wheeler loves choir drill. In her black cassock and small velvet cap she dreams of a cloistered life. Yet at home, in a rose hat and blue frock, by two her dreams turn to love.
the-consumer-viewpoint:
Mildred Maddocks, director of the Good Housekeeping Institute's Department of Household Engineering, sets out the buyer's side of making and selling household devices. A short note from C. Henry Hathaway explains that Good Housekeeping built reader-service departments to gauge what buyers need, and that the pages ahead share years of study in home appliances.

Maddocks stresses one odd fact about the trade: most goods made by men are also used by men, but home devices are made by men and used by women. That split, she says, puts the selling problems of the trade in a class of their own. Makers and dealers, her foreword adds, still grope for standards, since no one can predict the care and skill each device will meet in a home.
the-country-housewife-and-lady-s-directo: R. Bradley, professor of botany at Cambridge and fellow of the Royal Society, wrote The Country Housewife and Lady's Director, here in its sixth edition. The title promises guidance on the brew-house and malt liquors, wines of all sorts, and dairy work for butter and cheese on poor soils. It also covers fish, fowl, herbs, and roots for the table, distilling, ketchup, and durable sauces, arranged by month, with remarks on drying saffron. A dedication to Lady Wager follows. Only the title page and dedication are present here.
the-daughter-of-the-commandant:
Alexksandr Poushkin's Russian romance The Daughter of the Commandant comes to English readers in Mrs. Milne Home's translation. A preface signed M. P. M. H. and dated April 1891 calls the novel its author's best prose work in Russian eyes. It sketches his life: born at Petersburg in 1799 of good family, dead before forty in the prime of his genius.

The preface lists his Boris Godunof, The Prisoner of the Caucasus, and the poems The Gipsies, Ruslan and Ludmilla, and Evgeni Oneghin. Suspicion once banished him to a distant part of the empire; the Tzar Nicholai recalled him in 1825 and made him historiographer. Spiteful reports, the preface says, led to a duel in which his brother-in-law George Danthes wounded him to death, and all Russia mourned. The contents promise chapters on a sergeant of the guards, a duel, love, Pugatshef, and an assault.
the-defendant: G. K. Chesterton, author of The Wild Knight and Greybeards at Play, published The Defendant in a second London edition dated 1902 from R. Brimley Johnson. A note dated October 1901 explains that the defences in the volume first appeared in The Speaker and are reprinted, revised and enlarged, by the editor's leave. The contents list defences of penny dreadfuls, rash vows, skeletons, publicity, nonsense, planets, china shepherdesses, useful information, heraldry, ugly things, and farce, plus a defence of a new edition. Only the front matter and contents are present here.
the-einstein-theory-of-relativity-a-conc:
Prof. H. A. Lorentz of the University of Leyden gives a concise account of The Einstein Theory of Relativity in this small book. Its note says few may grasp the full theory, yet all want word of it, while most books demand high maths. Lorentz, whom Einstein credits with a share in the theory's growth, first printed his account in a Dutch paper of November 19, 1919.

He opens with the May 29 eclipse, whose measures backed Einstein's new law of gravity. Light bending near the sun proved the point. Plain words carry a hard idea here.
the-evolution-of-man-scientifically-disp:
Rev. William A. Williams's The Evolution of Man Scientifically Disproved sets out its market at the front. It is a text book, made to pair with evolution texts. It is an antidote to library books that teach infidelity. It is an aid to students, parents, and teachers. Ministers, lawyers, and doctors are named too. He adds a claim that man's evolution fails on maths alone.

Williams sorts the theories first: atheists hold matter eternal or chance-born, he says, and terms tangle from there. His fifty points then attack age, descent, and missing links. The book is a period piece of the anti-evolution push.
the-friendly-road-new-adventures-in-cont:
David Grayson, the pen name of Ray Stannard Baker, wrote The Friendly Road as new adventures in contentment, printed in 1913. It goes on from his Adventures in Friendship.

Grayson says the chapters grew from quiet walks on country roads, set down as they came. He recalls the folk of his roads: a country minister, the Stanleys, Bill Hahn the socialist, the Vedders in their garden, and a brush peddler. From his porch he looks out on fields and a curving town road, glad for the human cord that binds him to them all. The book praises slow travel and plain neighbors.
the-harris-ingram-experiment: Charles E. Bolton, M.A., wrote The Harris-Ingram Experiment, published in Cleveland by The Burrows Brothers Company in 1905. Bolton is named as the author of A Model Village and Other Papers and Travels in Europe and America, and the book is dedicated to his wife and son. Contents chapters include The Harrises in New York, Mr. Hugh Searles of London Arrives, A Bad Send-off, and Aboard the S.S. Majestic. Nothing past the front matter is present here.
the-high-deeds-of-finn-and-other-bardic-: T. W. Rolleston wrote The High Deeds of Finn and Other Bardic Romances of Ancient Ireland, with an introduction by Stopford A. Brooke and sixteen pictures by Stephen Reid, published in New York by Thomas Y. Crowell & Company. A note explains that one Finn tale, The Pursuit of Dermot and Grania, was left out in part because it shows Finn in a light at odds with the rest. The contents begin with The Story of the Children of Lir. Only the title page, note, and contents are present here.
the-irish-race-in-the-past-and-the-prese: The Reverend Aug. J. Thebaud, S.J., wrote this history of the Irish race. The pages present here hold only an old etext header. Nothing of the book itself appears. The header names the title and the author. License and donation boilerplate fills the rest. The text dates from around December 2000. No chapter, preface, or page of Thebaud's account can be read here. The record carries the wrapper and not the work. Ireland's past and present stay behind that wrapper.
the-king-s-achievement: Robert Hugh Benson signed this novel's acknowledgments at Cambridge on July 14, 1905. He thanked Dom Bede Camm and Mgr. Barnes for revising proofs, E. Conybeare for the cover's coins, and Abbot Gasquet for books and answers. Benson had written By What Authority before it. Only the preface matter and first contents are present here. The narrative itself does not appear. Book I, The King's Will, moves through a decision, the arrival at Lewes, Master More, and a merry prisoner. It is a Henrician story told from the Catholic side.
the-last-tournament:
Alfred Tennyson places his Arthurian poem between Pelleas and Guinevere among the Idylls of the King. Dagonet, the fool made mock knight by Gawain, dances before the hall at Camelot like a withered leaf. Tristram approaches with a harp and a swaying ruby necklace won in the jousts.

Tennyson then recalls how Arthur and Lancelot once found a crying babe in an eagle nest on a crag. The Queen raised the child, named Nestling, and loved her until early death. The ruby prize from that rescue now hangs over a court already touched by decay.
the-little-immigrant:
Eva Stern wrote The Little Immigrant in 1921, drawing on how her parents met, married, and began a family; the book was privately printed, and few copies survive. An introduction by her great-grandson explains that most names are thinly disguised. Her mother Ernestine, renamed Renestine in the story, is the little immigrant of the title, while General Buell appears under his real name from the Reconstruction years.

Chapter one shows thirteen-year-old Renestine packing her trunk at midnight, dreaming while her mother hurries her along. She is to sail to America to join a married sister already there. Readers get a family story of immigration told from inside, with a key that matches the invented names to the real people behind them.
the-living-present: Gertrude Atherton's The Living Present was published by Frederick A. Stokes Company and dedicated to Eternal France. Only the title page, frontispiece, and part of the contents are present here, so the text does not appear. The contents announce Book I, French Women in War Time. Its chapters include Madame Balli and the "Comfort Package," The Silent Army, and The Munition Makers. Others follow on Mademoiselle Javal and the Éclopés, Madame Pierre Goujon, Valentine Thompson, Madame Waddington, and the Countess d'Haussonville. The list closes with The Woman's Opportunity.
the-log-of-a-noncombatant:
Horace Green, staff correspondent of the New York Evening Post and special correspondent of the Boston Journal, wrote The Log of a Noncombatant in 1915. Chapter one finds him in the Post city room when war broke out in August 1914. A copy boy hands him a telegram from a Boston friend, Willard B. Luther, asking cryptically, "How about this fight?"

The contents map where that question took him: from Broadway to Ghent, the bombardment of Termonde, capture, the bombardment and surrender of Antwerp, and spying on spies. An appendix is titled Atrocities. Green writes as a civilian reporter caught inside a war zone, and his log mixes personal anecdote with front-line observation of Belgium's ordeal.
the-lost-continent:
Edgar Rice Burroughs wrote The Lost Continent, first published under the title Beyond Thirty. Its narrator admits a lifelong fascination with the last days of twentieth-century Europe. Two centuries have passed since contact between the Western and Eastern Hemispheres ceased after the Great War, and censored histories leave Europe's fate a matter of speculation.

He recounts how news still filtered west for fifteen years, until a slogan, "The East for the East, the West for the West," ended all intercourse by statute. Mine-strewn oceans had already killed transoceanic commerce. The last submarine sighted, he says, was the huge Q 138, which attacked a Brazilian tanker near the Bermudas with twenty-nine torpedoes in the fall of 1972. A companion record shares this title but holds a different author's Atlantis novel.
the-man-and-the-moment: Elinor Glyn's The Man and the Moment was published by D. Appleton and Company in 1914, illustrated by R. F. James. Only the title pages and list of illustrations are present, so the novel does not appear. The captions give the flavor. A frontispiece is captioned "It all looked intimate and lover-like." One plate shows a hero bounding forward to meet a heroine. Another shows a table near theirs in a restaurant. A line of dialogue worries that someone is in some scrape and that something must have culminated tonight.
the-moving-picture-boys-on-the-war-front:
Victor Appleton's The Moving Picture Boys on the War Front, subtitled The Hunt for the Stolen Army Films, was published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap with copyright in 1918. Only title page and the start of a contents list are present here, so the story does not appear. A frontispiece caption says it took all three lads' nerve to stand at their posts while men were killed around them.

Contents shown run only to Chapter VI, with page numbers. A Call to Battle starts at page 1, The Accident at page 11, and Monsieur Secor at page 20. All Aboard, Anxious Days, and A Queer Conference follow. Appleton is billed as author of the Tom Swift books on the title page.
the-muse-of-the-department:
Honore de Balzac's The Muse of the Department, translated by James Waring, opens with a dedication letter to the Count Ferdinand de Gramont. Balzac thanks Gramont for devising the coats of arms and mottoes of the great families in his Human Comedy. He calls the resulting armorial, or book of heraldry, a complete manual of French heraldry. He also calls it a monument of friendship and patience.

The novel then begins at Sancerre, a town crowning hills above the Loire on the edge of Le Berry. The river floods the flats below, leaving fertile yellow alluvium, the rich soil rivers deposit, except where a terrible rising has buried fields in sand forever. The little river-port of Saint-Thibault draws its life from the Loire at the hill's foot.
the-new-york-subway-its-construction-and:
The New York Subway: Its Construction and Equipment was issued by the Interborough Rapid Transit Company in New York, with copyright in 1904, and planned and executed by the McGraw Publishing Company. Only a title page and the start of a table of contents are present here, so the engineering chapters do not appear. Illustrations of the power house operating room and the company symbol head the pages.

Contents shown give page numbers for an introduction at page 13 and five chapters. The Route of the Road, covering passenger stations and tracks, begins at page 23. Types and Methods of Construction follow at page 37, the power house building at page 67, and the power plant, from coal pile to engine shafts, at page 77.
the-number-concept-its-origin-and-develo:
Levi Leonard Conant, a mathematics professor at Worcester Polytechnic Institute, wrote a study of how number ideas began and grew. The Macmillan Company published the book in New York and London. Conant looks at counting systems from many peoples rather than only the familiar decimal one.

Tables in the book give numeral words in Hebrew, Tahuatan, Bagrimma, Nahuatl, and other languages. Some systems count by fives, others by twenties, and the largest Nahuatl terms reach into the millions. By setting these systems side by side, Conant shows that counting is a human invention shaped by hands, trade, and custom, not a gift handed down in one form.
the-origin-and-permanent-value-of-the-ol: Charles Foster Kent, Woolsey Professor of Biblical Literature at Yale University, wrote The Origin and Permanent Value of the Old Testament. Only the contents are present here, so the chapters themselves do not appear. The list runs to sixteen chapters. It opens with The Eclipse and Rediscovery of the Old Testament. Later chapters treat the prophetic histories, the Hebrew sages and their proverbs, and the history of the Psalter. The formation of the canon and practical methods of study close the list.
the-pawns-count:
E. Phillips Oppenheim published The Pawns Count in 1918. A foreword lines up four voices: John Lutchester for England only, Nikasti for Japan only, Oscar Fischer for Germany first and America afterwards, and Pamela Van Teyl for America always. They were all right, the foreword says, except the German-American.

Chapter One opens in a fashionable London restaurant. Pamela, a beautiful American girl, points to a wall notice in French warning that enemy ears listen. Except for wounded companions, she says, it is the first thing in England that makes her realize the country is at war. A spy tale of the First World War begins over luncheon.
the-pianoforte-sonata-its-origin-and-dev: J. S. Shedlock's The Pianoforte Sonata traces the form in eleven chapters, published in London by Methuen and Co. Only the title page and contents appear here, so the chapter text is absent. The contents move from an opening chapter through Johann Kuhnau and his contemporary Bernardo Pasquini. Later chapters cover Emanuel Bach, Haydn and Mozart, and the men who came just before Beethoven. Closing chapters treat Beethoven, then Schumann, Chopin, Brahms, and Liszt, the sonata in England, and modern sonatas.
the-power-of-womanhood-or-mothers-and-so: Ellice Hopkins wrote The Power of Womanhood, or Mothers and Sons as a book for parents and those in a parent's place. E. P. Dutton and Company published it at New York, with an 1899 copyright. Hopkins is named as author of a life of James Hinton. What is shown here is the title page and the first page of the contents. Early chapters are headed Introductory, Why Should I Interfere?, First Principles, and The Secret and Method. Early Boyhood and Boyhood and School Life follow.
the-principles-of-scientific-management:
Frederick Winslow Taylor's Principles of Scientific Management, dated 1911, opens by quoting President Roosevelt: conservation of national resources is only preliminary to national efficiency. Forests vanish and coal and iron run out in plain sight, Taylor argues. The larger waste, of human effort through blundering and ill-directed work, leaves nothing visible behind. It calls for memory and imagination to grasp, though the daily loss exceeds the waste of materials.

No public agitation for greater efficiency has yet arisen, yet the need is widely felt. The search for competent men, from company presidents to household servants, was never more vigorous, and demand exceeds supply. What everyone seeks, Taylor says, is the ready-made competent man trained by someone else. The duty and opportunity lie instead in training men systematically.
the-professional-aunt:
Mary C. E. Wemyss's narrator in The Professional Aunt had her profession forced on her by her sisters-in-law and their children. Zerlina holds that one woman in every family should be a professional aunt, a post giving full scope to any reasonable woman's energies. An aunt who marries loses her perfecting at once, exchanging a fitted profession for a lottery. Zerlina's aunt must remember every nephew's and niece's birthday, which by her reasoning leads to presents.

The successful aunt also knows each child's particular taste, and the exact moment that taste changes. The narrator writes from Zerlina's point of view throughout this opening chapter. Professions, she observes, are often chosen for boys by parents, which is why shrewd boys become painters and artistic ones join the Stock Exchange. Her own calling came by family appointment rather than choice.
the-re-creation-of-brian-kent:
Harold Bell Wright frames his Ozark story with a long letter to his Auntie Sue, dated April 30, 1919, at Riverside, California. He teases her that she will deny ever living in a little log house by a river in the Ozark Mountains, then asks whether she is quite sure she never did.

Wright says he will be heartbroken if readers do not love her, and notes she will turn eighty-seven the next November. A verse from John Dyer about rivers running to the deep follows the letter. The dedication itself tells readers the book will treat an old woman's goodness as the center of a simple story of life and love.
the-regent:
Arnold Bennett calls his 1913 novel a Five Towns story of adventure in London. Edward Henry Machin walks home to Bleakridge at six minutes to six, reflecting that despite everything he does not feel so jolly after all.

Contents promise a dog-bite, a bank-note, entry into the theatrical world, titled hosts, a cornerstone, a first night, and a woman named Isabel. Bennett sends a provincial businessman into London theatre management, where money and art collide. The rueful opening mood promises comedy built on respectability shaken loose from home ground at last.
the-reminiscences-of-an-irish-land-agent: S. M. Hussey's reminiscences were compiled by Home Gordon and published at London by Duckworth in 1904 with two portraits. Contents move from ancestry, parentage, and education through farming and work as a land agent in Cork to famine and fever, then Fenianism. Here only the title pages and opening of the contents list are present, so the reminiscences themselves do not appear.
the-research-magnificent:
H. G. Wells published his novel in 1915, opening with a prelude on fear and aristocracy. William Porphyry Benham, readers learn, was led into adventure by an idea that possessed his imagination early and grew with him until it interwove with his whole being.

Benham had money enough to follow the idea around the world, into situations bordering on the fantastic that made him ridiculous and nearly sublime. Contents promise boyhood, town life, a wife named Amanda, a spirited honeymoon, and jealousy judged. Wells turns a life story into the biography of a ruling thought.
the-room-in-the-dragon-volant:
J. Sheridan LeFanu frames The Room in the Dragon Volant as a curious case. Its prologue says the case is referred to in an essay by Doctor Hesselius. That essay treats the drug lore of the Dark and Middle Ages.

Hesselius titled his essay Mortis Imago. He discussed the Vinum letiferum and the Beatifica. He also covered the Somnus Angelorum. About twenty other infusions and distillations appear in his list. Sages knew them eight hundred years earlier. Two of them, he alleges, remain known to a fraternity of thieves. Police-office inquiries sometimes support that claim, the prologue says. The frame promises a story where old drugs meet present crime.
the-russian-revolution-the-jugo-slav-mov:
Russian Revolution gathers pieces by four named writers. They are Alexander Petrunkevitch, Samuel Northrup, Harper Frank, and Alfred Golder. The volume also contains The Jugo-Slav Movement by Robert Joseph Kerner. The portion shown is Petrunkevitch's essay of March 18, 1918. Its subject is the role of intellectuals in Russia's liberating movement.

Petrunkevitch quotes a November interview with Leon Trotzky. He defended the Bolshevik coup in that interview. He claimed workers, soldiers, and peasants stood with the government. Petrunkevitch sets that claim against a private letter. His father Ivan wrote the letter in June. The elder Petrunkevitch had led the Constitutional Democrats in the first Duma. His son argues the Council was led by intellectuals. They were well educated men, unlike the masses they claimed to represent.
the-saint:
Antonio Fogazzaro's novel The Saint reached American readers under unusual circumstances, explained in a publisher's note dated New York, July 1906. The Congregation of the Index had condemned the book. The American publishers had secured Fogazzaro's sanction for their authorized translation before that sentence passed. As a loyal Catholic he could not have given it later. Once given, he did not feel justified in withdrawing it.

A further note prepares readers for the hero. Piero Maironi, the Saint, appeared in Fogazzaro's earlier romances. His wife was in a lunatic asylum. He had fallen in love with Jeanne Dessalle, a woman separated from her husband. A deathbed interview with his wife recalled him to faith and honour. He vanished from his friends after leaving a sealed paper with a priest. That paper described a prophetic vision behind his conversion.
the-stolen-white-elephant:
Mark Twain frames this comic tale as a curious history. A chance railway acquaintance told it to him. The man was an elderly official of the Indian civil service. Twain notes that the piece was left out of A Tramp Abroad. Doubts about its truth kept it out. The King of Siam, making reparation after a frontier dispute with Great Britain, sent the Queen a transcendentally royal present: a sacred white elephant.

The narrator conveyed the animal to Jersey City, where it was to recover its health before sailing. A fortnight later the elephant was stolen. The terrified official rushed to New York's detective headquarters. The celebrated Inspector Blunt was just leaving. The hunt launches Twain's satire on detective method and official fuss.
the-story-of-a-stuffed-elephant: Laura Lee Hope's Make Believe story of a stuffed elephant was published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York, illustrated by Harry L. Smith, under a 1922 copyright. The pages present here hold the cover and title pages. The first line of a contents list follows. It opens with a chapter called The Elephant and the Mouse on page one. The elephant's own adventures do not appear.
the-strolling-saint: Rafael Sabatini's historical novel of 1913, reissued by Barnes and Noble in a 2011 edition, is presented here through its contents alone. The same contents appear in two companion records. They carry the book's fuller title, the confessions of Agostino D'Anguissola. A first book, The Oblate, leads off. Its chapters cover Gino Falcone and a pietistic thrall. Luisina, rebellion, and Fra Gervasio follow. A second book, Giuliana, opens at the house of Astorre Fifanti. Sabatini's narrative itself does not appear.
the-triumphs-of-euge-ne-valmont: Robert Barr's Triumphs of Eugène Valmont collects eight cases for his French detective. This record gives the contents list. A note says the attribution and table were added by the transcriber. Cases promise the mystery of the five hundred diamonds. They offer a bomb-thrower's Siamese twin and the clue of the silver spoons. Lord Chizelrigg's missing fortune, a ghost with a club-foot, and Lady Alicia's emeralds follow. An appendix adds two Sherlock Holmes parodies, Sherlaw Kombs among them. Valmont's own narration begins beyond these pages.
the-voyage-of-governor-phillip-to-botany:
John Stockdale published The Voyage of Governor Phillip to Botany Bay in London in 1789. The volume was compiled from authentic papers obtained from government departments. It adds the journals of Lieutenants Shortland, Watts, and Ball and Captain Marshall, with fifty-five copper plates and charts from actual surveys.

Stockdale dedicates the book to the Marquis of Salisbury, calling it everything so far known about the Sydney Cove settlement. Anecdotes of Governor Phillip follow, describing an officer who rose by merit like Drake, Dampier, and Cook. Phillip's father, Jacob, came from Frankfort and taught languages in England, while his mother, Elizabeth Breach, had first married a naval captain.
the-war-chief-of-the-six-nations-a-chron:
Louis Aubrey Wood chronicles Joseph Brant in The War Chief of the Six Nations, volume sixteen of the Chronicles of Canada. Published at Toronto in 1915, the book follows Brant from young Mohawk to statesman of the tribes. Contents chapters include the battle of Lake George, schooldays, Fort Stanwix and Oriskany, Cherry Valley, Minisink, and a final church bell.

Chapter one camps huntsmen along the Ohio river under moonlight, fires darting among the trees. Hunters strip prey and ready weapons while women move in the dancing shadows. One woman bends over a newborn infant and speaks his name into the still evening. Wood begins Brant's life inside the forest world his wars would shake, before England, school, and revolution divide his ways.
the-well-beloved-a-sketch-of-a-temperame:
Thomas Hardy calls The Well-Beloved a sketch of a temperament, and his preface describes its setting as a peninsula carved by time from a single stone. That isle has housed for centuries a distinct people with strange beliefs and singular customs, now mostly fading. Fancies grow there naturally, Hardy says, like soft-wooded plants that need sea air.

His hero is a native of natives who gives a name and continuity to a delicate dream common to all men, familiar already to Platonic philosophers. Hardy warns that verisimilitude is subordinated to this ideal, subjective aim. He also records the tale's history: serialised in 1892 under another title, it first appeared independently in 1897.
thoughts-on-religion-at-the-front: The Rev. Neville S. Talbot, assistant chaplain-general and late of the Rifle Brigade, wrote Thoughts on Religion at the Front. Macmillan published it in 1917 in London, New York, Toronto, and other cities. Talbot had been fellow and chaplain of Balliol and wrote The Mind of the Disciples. The edition was reprinted three times during 1917, in March, April, and November. The title and publication pages are what is shown in this record, so Talbot's front-line reflections themselves are not shown.
umboo-the-elephant: Howard R. Garis's Umboo, the Elephant belongs to his Circus Animal Stories, from the author of the Uncle Wiggily series. The contents follow Umboo from babyhood through fifteen chapters. He travels on the march, picks nuts, gets lost, meets a snake, and is caught in a trap. Later he goes to school, is sold, shipped, and at last reaches the circus. Only the title page and contents are present here, so Umboo's story itself does not appear.
un-doc-rio-declaration-on-environment-an:
World leaders at the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro adopted this declaration, a short United Nations text of twenty-seven principles on environment and development. It came out of the largest gathering of heads of government held up to that time. Its aim was to link care for nature with the fight against poverty.

The principles say states may use their own resources but must not harm other states. They call for public access to information, action to cut poverty, and care that guards future generations. The declaration still frames talks on climate, forests, and fair growth today.
un-doc-yalta-conference-agreement:
Leaders of the United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union met at Yalta in February 1945 and produced this agreement on the postwar world. Franklin Roosevelt, Winston Churchill, and Joseph Stalin bargained as the Second World War neared its end in Europe. Their choices shaped the map for decades.

The text covers the division of defeated Germany into zones of occupation. It sets terms for Poland, for war trials, and for Soviet entry into the war on Japan. It also confirms plans to found the United Nations. Few short texts carry more weight in modern history.
webster-s-seventh-of-march-speech-and-th:
Herbert Darling Foster studied Webster's Seventh of March Speech and the secession movement of 1850. His paper came from the American Historical Review of January 1922, with a foreword by Nathaniel Wright Stephenson. Stephenson marvels that so much of the history of the eighteen forties and fifties has slipped from general memory. Nine of ten Americans, he guesses, would strain to place that famous speech among the nation's political adventures.

He lists what an honest exam would demand. The Wilmot Proviso comes first, meant to make free soil of the land to be won in the Mexican War. The instant, bitter southern reaction follows. Plans to split the conquered ground between slave and free labor come next. The gold seekers of California in 1849 made a free state with no leave from Congress. Foster's study then takes up Webster's great compromise speech itself, and the storm it raised.
what-eight-million-women-want: Only the front pages are present here, so the chapters themselves do not appear. Rheta Childe Dorr published What Eight Million Women Want in 1910, for the members of the General Federation of Women's Clubs. The contents move from culture clubs to social service, then to women and the law. Later chapters take up factories, the servant question, and votes for women. Her pieces first ran in Hampton's Magazine. Readers see her full plan, chapter by chapter, but not the text.
with-british-guns-in-italy-a-tribute-to-: The pages here present the title page, dedications, and the start of a contents list for Hugh Dalton's With British Guns in Italy, first published in 1919, with no war narrative shown. Dalton had served as a lieutenant in the Royal Garrison Artillery. He gives the book to the cause of Anglo-Italian friendship. Quotes from Pericles' funeral speech and from Meredith head the work. The contents open with the Anglo-Italian tradition and Italy's part in the war. Twelve pictures and three maps aid the book.
with-wolfe-in-canada-the-winning-of-a-co:
G. A. Henty wrote this 1894 historical novel about the British fight for Canada. His preface tells young readers why the struggle mattered. England held only a narrow strip on the east coast. France held Canada, Louisiana, and a chain of forts between them. That wall shut English settlers out of the west.

The chapter list follows one hero through rescues, battles, and scouting. Named stops include Braddock's defeat, Lake George, Fort William Henry, Louisbourg, and Quebec. The final chapters cover the climb to the heights and the capture of Quebec under Wolfe. War history drives the plot throughout.
woman-suffrage-by-federal-constitutional:
Carrie Chapman Catt compiled this 1917 case for a federal voting amendment. The volume is dedicated to Congress and the state legislatures. Catt argues that no state should deny the vote because of sex. Her own chapter lists seven reasons for federal action. She notes that state constitutions can be nearly impossible to amend. Election fraud also goes unchecked, she says.

Mary Sumner Boyd's chapter then details recent defeats caused by legal technicalities. Other chapters gather testimony from supporters across public life. Readers get a campaign handbook, not a neutral history. Its goal was to win the amendment fight.
